en: (296v/596) With reference to the circle of yoginīs beginning with Nairātmyā, he speaks—starting with "Now" (*atha*)—for the purpose of explaining [the practice] according to the middle sequence. The compiler [of the tantra] states that he will speak exactly as it was briefly taught by the Blessed One. By the expression "the space-element" (*khadhātu*), one yoga consisting of the realization of emptiness is shown. Its constituent parts, however, should be understood as the meditations taught in the seventh [chapter], beginning with the seat and the seed-syllable at the heart and ending with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
By the phrase "a sun-maṇḍala in the center of the space-element," [the subsequent visualization] beginning with "the sun in front by means of the syllable *repha*" is indicated.

The *vajrapañjara* is for the purpose of gathering the seed-syllables (*bīja*). Following that, one should visualize the *dharmodaya-mudrā*—which has become empty through the previously performed worship, which is instantly perceived as the transformation of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), which is triangular because of its similarity to the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*), and which is white as the autumn moon because it is free from all obscurations—and which is great and triangular because its nature is the Vajradhara who consists of the three bodies (*kāyatraya*). In the center of that, one should contemplate the foundation wheel (*ādhāracakra*). To the question "How? he says: "The wheel" refers to the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*).

"First" means initially. "According to rule" means without transgressing the proper order, such as the transformation of earth and so forth. "Immediately after that, according to the arising of the deities"—this implies that one should contemplate [the sequence] without skipping the five aspects. He explains this summary: "The wheel" refers to the maṇḍala, which is connected everywhere, such as the earth-maṇḍala, the water-maṇḍala, and so on.

"First" means that, in relation to the circles of fire and wind, the priority and posteriority of the circles of earth and water should be understood precisely according to the order of their description. "In due order" refers to this principle: fire is to be visualized above the circle of wind, water above that, and the circle of earth above that; for such is the arrangement of the circles of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*). The phrase "of the deities" should also be connected to every instance [in the preceding text].

These maṇḍalas are to be understood as having the same form as those deities—Locanā and the others—who are the respective manifestations of purity. As for the seed-syllables of wind and the other elements, they are the syllables YAṂ, RAṂ, VAṂ, and LAṂ.

And as for the "meditator," he should be viewed as being of the nature of the bodhicitta inseparable from emptiness and compassion; appearing just as it arises, without deviating from its arising, like one who has emanated the mandalas of earth and the other elements. Regarding the phrase "arisen from the source of phenomena" (*dharmodayodbhava*): it means that its arising or production occurs within the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*). By implication, the "wheel" is the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) born from the dissolution of the four great elements. It is "double-layered" because it is endowed with two layers demarcated by a garland of vajras. It is "pure" because of its translucence, and "free from affliction" because of its faultlessness.

"One [should be] with the filaments" means that the inner enclosure (*garbhapuṭa*) is an eight-petaled lotus characterized by its filaments. "The Vajra-holder who bears the three bodies" refers to the Vajra-holder whose nature is the three bodies; this means that outside the central lotus, within the interior of the palace situated in the *dharmodayā*—which is triangular in form and consists of the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*)—there is a second outer enclosure. Its qualities, such as being square and so forth, will be explained later. The seats are moon-maṇḍalas.

"Of that" refers to the corpse; "upon [it], in the heart, is the moon. Regarding "the sun is stepped upon": it means one should subsequently visualize the sun as having been stepped upon—that is, the seed-syllable situated on the moon is positioned above the sun. As was stated previously: "The row of moons, the letter *kā*, and the sun—the seed-syllable should be situated in the middle. "The union of the two is great bliss"—the remainder of the phrase is "presided over by consciousness," because it has been experienced in such a way at birth and so forth.
And here, in this very manner, this conjunction of the moon and sun is meditated upon as being presided over by the seed-syllables of consciousness and form.

He states the seed-syllables of the moon and sun with the words beginning "sthitā" (abiding). Those two [syllables] are the transformations of *āli* and *kāli*. He states that the generation of Gaurī and the others occurs in exactly the same way with the words beginning "candre" (on the moon). The mere meeting of the moon and sun is referred to as such by metaphorically applying the name of the effect to the cause. Although one should have said "Vajrā and the others," he says "Gaurī and the others" in order to exclude the notion of sequential generation, because all of them arise simultaneously.

[Objection: Is it not the case that Buddhahood results from the fivefold realization consisting of the five wisdoms (*pañcajñāna*), and not from the meditation on the moon and so forth? To this, he says: "The mirror," and so on. A mirror (*ādarśa*) is that in which reflections appear according to their respective forms; it is a clear surface such as a looking-glass. Likewise, a wisdom that is exceedingly clear is called mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). That [wisdom] exists in which the world appears like a reflection in a mirror. Because [the moon] exists in identity with that, the moon is "possessed of mirror-like wisdom."

The meaning is that the cultivation of the moon (*candrabhāvanā*) is itself the cultivation of the mirror (*ādarśabhāvanā*). The intention is that the mind, which is extremely clear, is the very form of the moon—the mirror for the entire world. It is the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*) by means of which one realizes the equality of the world reflected therein. That which consists of this is the sun of the seven-times-seven knowledge of equality; it is so called because it possesses seven times seven—that is, forty-nine—horses. The meaning is that the cultivation of the sun (*sūryabhāvanā*) is itself the cultivation of the knowledge of equality (*samatājñānabhāvanā*).

At the conjunction of the moon and sun, because all phenomena are like reflections, there is no perception of difference even within the mind consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). This is the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), by which, while thus absorbed in meditative equipoise, one discerns the mental activities of all sentient beings. In this context, the observation of one's own deity through its seed-syllables and signs is called "discernment."

The meaning is that the *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (discriminating awareness) is characterized by the signs of one’s own deity, which arise from seed-syllables (*bīja*) and are presided over by seed-syllables. For its intention is that it manifests as the supreme discernment of the welfare of the world.

The plural number in "by seed-syllables" (*bījair*) is due to the multiplicity of the seed-syllables of the goddesses. The singular number in "the sign" (*cihnam*) is because the sign—the blue vajra—is one for all fifteen [goddesses]. It is called "the performance of activities" (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*) because, having thus discerned the world, it carries out the welfare of beings through immeasurable emanations.

Therefore, in this context, a single practice is taught by all [the tantras]. "By all" means that through the emanations of the seed-syllables and signs of the moon and sun, there is oneness with the worlds; this is the state of being of equal flavor (*samarasībhāva*) because of the complete cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). This is the "awakening in a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇābhisaṃbodha*) here, because in one single moment there is such awakening regarding the entire world as being devoid of all conceptual proliferation. Thus, it is called the "accomplishment of the image through purification."

Immediately following that is the perfection of the form of the deity, which means the thoroughly pure gnosis of the dharmadhātu (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*). This is because that [deity] itself consists of the nature of the thoroughly pure gnosis of the dharmadhātu. The beginner [attains this] through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) by means of the fivefold forms consisting of the five gnoses, described according to the prescribed methods such as the moon and so forth. However, one who has attained some degree of perfection, through those very same prescribed methods, achieves some direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of that object.

In this context, although the cause consists of the four gnoses (*jñāna*), there is indeed an *ādhimokṣika* great bliss (*mahāsukha*). For this very reason, this cause is called Vajradhara. Even in the fivefold manifest enlightenment (*pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi*), there is *ādhimokṣika* great bliss; therefore, it is through the integration with the Goddess that the arising of Vajradhara is the perfection of the fivefold manifest enlightenment of great bliss. That itself is, in reality, the fivefold manifest enlightenment, and that very thing is shown here in the maṇḍala of Nairātmyā-Heruka.

In this context, however, within the maṇḍala of selflessness (*nairātmyā*), great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is to be understood through instruction, yet it does not manifest all at once (*dhag ity*) in such a manner. For this very reason, this is taught as the intermediate stage. When there is the union of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya-sampuṭa*), that [bliss] becomes perfectly clear; therefore, this is taught as the superior stage. Consequently, even though the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*) is described in other tantras by way of the sequence beginning with the moon and so forth, its nature as great bliss is not explicitly taught therein.

In such Yoga and Yoginī tantras alone is the stage of the Vajra-holder, consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), clearly manifest. Subsequently, although it is understood from the essential point even elsewhere, it is not taught there except through the initiation of the co-emergent (*sahaja-seka*). This is solely by the command of the Blessed One. Indeed, the initiation of the co-emergent occurs only in such tantras as these.

He says, "Without the Causal Vajradhara, there is no arising of the Fruitional Vajradhara," beginning with the words *ālī* and so forth. *Viṣṭara* means a seat. Here, the Causal Vajradhara is in the form of a seed-syllable situated within the emblem located between the moon and the sun. Regarding the *piṇḍa* (body) of Vajrasattva which arises from the syllable: the syllable *HŪṂ*, which is pronounced at the time of moving the lotus, and the yellow *PHAṬ* syllable, which is being visualized for the retention of the bodhicitta at the two apertures of the tip of the vajra, are not accepted here because they are not appropriate; this is the remainder of the sense.

"Arising from the reflection of sentient beings" means produced from the Vajradhara mentioned immediately above. "Lord of the mandala" refers to Nairātmyā. This has been stated: the four gnoses are the cause and the five are the fruit. Therefore, is the resultant Vajradhara not composed of the five gnoses? It is not so; for these [five], which are purified through purification, arise in that very form. Through the sequence of the emergence of the sense faculties and so forth, and through the sequence of radiating and reabsorbing, those very [gnoses] are seen as perfectly pure.

"As before" means that for the purpose of worship, confession of sins, and so forth, it is like the introduction of selflessness (*nairātmyāvat*). For Vajragarbha was first instructed by the Blessed One regarding the facial marks, ornaments, and so on, and subsequently [the teaching] was compiled; however, out of fear of redundancy, it was done only later, specifically by the command of the Blessed One. This was with the intention that the Blessed One himself, acting as the Guru, should first provide the instruction.

The moonstone (*candrakānta*) jewel is without flaw and resembles the full moon; that whose radiance is like its radiance is "Moon-Radiant" (*Candraprabha*). This is also an elliptical designation for the seat; thus, even though she is fierce, the meaning is "the Goddess seated on the Moon-seat, Moon-Radiant. "In this way, all [are so]" refers to the other fourteen yoginīs. "By virtue of being the nature of wisdom and means" means that they consist of those very [qualities] because of their identity with the gnosis of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) and the gnosis of performance (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).

This very point is explained by the passage beginning with "the flow of wisdom" (*prajñālī*). Regarding "the distinction of colors": the distinction of seed-syllables (*bījabheda*) for the Vajra and the others is, respectively, *āṃ īṃ īṃ uṃ aṃ ḷṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḹṃ aiṃ aṃ*. By the phrase "by way of the nature of the five aggregates," he shows that the Yoginīs are to be meditated upon as having the nature of the purity of their respective objects, and not merely as this [single] form. Gaurī and the others are situated at the cardinal directions starting with the Vajra; Pukkasī and the others are situated in the corners starting from the northeast (*īśāna*), proceeding in a clockwise direction.

She runs and she protects, thus she is *adhavatī*. One is *ūrdhvavatī*. Who, then, are they? He says: *khecarī* and *bhūcarī*. *Bhūcarī* is situated by way of the nature of cyclic existence (*bhava*) because her movement is downward; for this very reason, she is downward-facing. *Khecarī* is situated by way of the nature of nirvāṇa because her movement is upward; for this very reason, she is upward-facing. Regarding "situated at the side": *Bhūcarī* is below and on the western side of Nairātmyā; *Khecarī* is above and on the eastern side.

"Those of all colors" refers to the eight [deities] situated in the outer enclosure, like the sixteen-armed maṇḍala; they possess colors such as yellow and so forth. The qualifiers beginning with "greatly fierce" apply to all of them. The specific details, however, are found in the root text itself. Cakrī and the others are located on the head, ears, neck, hands, and hips. "Of such a kind" means excluding the similarity of blue color. To the question "What is Nairātmyā like?", he says: "Yogapātrī" means a skull-cup filled with blood. "Blazing and radiant" means blazing in body and radiant in mind. "Blue-colored" means...

By this it is stated that the *bhūcarīs* and *khecarīs* residing within the inner enclosure (*adhyātmapuṭa*) are blue. "She" refers to Nairātmyā. Just as in the sixteen-armed maṇḍala, here too the female gatekeepers and the goddesses of worship are to be understood [in the same way]. However, he states the distinction: "On the right," and so forth. This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the east and west as well. There, at the eastern gate is Hayāsyā, white-blue; on the south is Sūkarāsyā, yellow-blue; on the west is Śvānāsyā, red-blue; and on the north is Siṃhāsyā, crimson-blue.

All four of these also hold a skull-bowl and a staff in their two hands; they have one face each, corresponding to their names. The qualifiers "smiling," "non-angry," and "erotic" apply to all twenty-three goddesses. Regarding the nature of their worship: in the corners starting from the northeast, the goddesses Vaṃśā, Vīṇā, Mukundā, and Murajā are to be understood as before. By this, the triad of yogas beginning with emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is taught.

He now describes the fourth yoga, which is to be cultivated immediately following that, beginning with the words "three," and so forth. The syllables *oṃ*, *āḥ*, and *hūṃ* are the essential natures of the three principles (*tattva*). One should join oneself to these at the head, throat, and heart. Regarding the term "middle": it means abiding in the middle seat, having considered that through this [yoga] there is the accomplishment of one's own and others' welfare. This is the sequence of realization (*abhisamaya*) here.

Having worshipped the Nairātmyā-maṇḍala—drawn by the rays of the seed-syllable in one’s own heart—together with the eight goddesses, and having performed the confession of sins and so forth up to the [construction of the] peaked pavilion, one should meditate there upon a two-layered maṇḍala containing twenty-three corpse-seats. Upon the moon on the chest of each corpse, one should visualize the twenty-three yoginīs, who have arisen from the transformation of the moon, sun, their respective seed-syllables, and symbols produced from the *āli* and *kāli* vowels and consonants.

Thereafter, having visualized the empowerment of the eyes and so forth, up to the [water] empowerment, according to the *Abhisamaya* of the three Herukas, one should contemplate that Nairātmyā, Vajragaurī, Vārī, and Vajraḍākinī are with Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi; Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, and Ghasmarī are with Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Ratnasaṃbhava, and Amitābha; Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī are with Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Ratnasaṃbhava, and Amitābha; Bhūcarī is with Vairocana; Khecarī is with Amitābha; and Hayāsyā and the others are bound by Vajrāṅkuśī and the rest.

The bamboo flutes and other instruments should be consecrated with seals, just like the maṇḍala of Vajrasattva. Beyond that, everything else should be understood as it is taught in the *Herukatrayābhisamaya*.
The eleventh mañjarī in the Āmnāyamañjarī, the commentary on the Śrīsampuṭa.
